1: In model inference, if we consider only the simplest scenario—running it on our own GPU and asking a few questions ourselves—the answers all come back quite fast. But once it is integrated into a business, it becomes a completely different scenario. At the same time, hundreds or thousands of people may be asking questions, and an Agent completing a task must call the model more than a dozen times in succession. SGLang is a large-scale inference framework born for exactly such scenarios: it deploys models as stable, efficient services and provides low-cost, high-quality tokens.
2: This chapter introduces the basic usage of SGLang: deploy a 4B model on the free GPU of ModelScope Notebook, call it with Python, and then see how much faster SGLang is when multiple people ask questions at the same time.
4: SGLang is an open-source large model inference framework. It loads the model onto the GPU and exposes an interface compatible with the OpenAI API. Business applications only need to send requests and get answers; how requests are queued and how they are computed on the GPU is all left to SGLang.
5: SGLang has already been used at large scale in production environments. Its users include technology companies such as NVIDIA, AMD, Google, Meta, Microsoft AI, and LinkedIn, as well as domestic vendors such as Alibaba Cloud, Tencent Cloud, Baidu, Meituan, Ant Group, Volcano Engine, and iFlytek, and universities such as Tsinghua University, Stanford, and UC Berkeley.
6: Compared with generating one by one directly with transformers, SGLang has mainly focused its efforts on two things.
7: First, it combines requests that arrive at the same time into one computation. Each time the model generates a token, it must read the entire model's weights from GPU memory once. When serving only one request, one read produces only one token, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data. SGLang groups multiple requests that are being generated into a batch, reads the weights once, and computes one token for each request in the batch; requests leave as soon as they finish writing, and new requests can join at any time. This approach is called Continuous Batching.
8: Second, identical prefixes are computed only once. In real business, many requests have the same beginning: every request in knowledge-base Q&A and customer service carries the same system prompt and materials; in multi-turn conversations, each question requires resending all previous chat history; each time an Agent calls a tool, it must send the entire previous process to the model again. If everything were computed from scratch each time, most of the compute would be spent on repeated content.
9: SGLang's approach is RadixAttention: the intermediate results computed when the model processes input are called KV Cache. After a request finishes, SGLang does not rush to discard them; instead, it organizes them into a Radix Tree by text prefix. Requests with the same beginning share the same branch on the tree and diverge where the content starts to differ. When a new request comes in, it first follows the tree to find the longest part that matches its own beginning, reuses that part directly, and computes only the newly added content afterward. The more conversation turns there are and the longer the shared prompt, the more computation is saved, and the faster the first token comes out.
10: RadixAttention is one of the core technologies proposed in the SGLang paper (NeurIPS 2024). It is enabled by default in SGLang and requires no code changes.
11: How noticeable is the effect? We ran a real test with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507: a single H200, BF16 precision, replaying two real work traces of an AI coding assistant (from the AgentX dataset publicly released by SemiAnalysis, taking the first 8 requests from each, with input length shortened to 1/16 of the original), 16 requests in total, with 2 sessions concurrent. The control group was Hugging Face Transformers serve with continuous batching and prefix caching enabled.
27: Same model, same GPU, switched to SGLang, and both throughput and latency differ by an order of magnitude. This was a small-scale test, only one round was run, and answer quality was not evaluated, but it is enough to show the role of the inference framework.

48: The number of tokens generated by the two methods is about the same. Sending one by one took 26.7 seconds, while sending simultaneously took only 2.4 seconds, and the number of tokens generated per second rose from 53 to 581. 16 people asking questions at the same time is not 16 times slower; instead, the overall speed is more than ten times faster. This is the continuous batching discussed earlier at work: multiple requests share the same computation, and the GPU's compute power is used more fully.
49: We also ran this test on a data-center-grade NVIDIA B300 with the same model and the same code, and compared the results from the two cards side by side:
62: The B300 has much higher compute power and memory bandwidth, and sending one by one is already more than 7 times faster than on the A10. 16 requests are still far from enough to fully load the B300, so the speedup factor for simultaneous sending is actually smaller than on the A10. Whichever card you switch to, the pattern is the same: the more requests arrive at the same time, the greater the benefit of SGLang computing them together.
64: If you see an out-of-memory (VRAM) warning at startup, lower --mem-fraction-static to around 0.7, or reduce --context-length; if the model itself does not fit, switch to a smaller model or a quantized version, see Chapter 13.
65: If you see CUDA errors such as CUDA driver version is insufficient at startup, it is usually because the instance is using an old CUDA 12.1 image. Stop the instance, switch to a CUDA 13.0 image under "Current Image Version", restart, and then install again.
66: If installation is very slow or hangs, confirm that you are using the pip bundled with the image. Tools such as uv access pypi.org by default, which is very slow on ModelScope instances. Also, do not create the environment under /mnt/workspace, for the reasons described above.
67: If you see a sglang command not found error after restarting the instance, the environment was created on the local disk and is cleared when the instance is stopped; just run the installation command again. The model is under /mnt/workspace and does not need to be downloaded again.
68: If you see FlashInfer-related errors at startup, add --attention-backend triton --sampling-backend pytorch to the startup command to switch to other implementations.
69: If you see address already in use, the port is occupied, usually because a previous service is still running. Stop the old service, or use a different port and update the port in the calling code accordingly.
70: After the experiment, press Ctrl + C in the terminal running the service to stop SGLang, then return to the Notebook page to stop the GPU instance. Closing only the browser page does not stop the cloud instance.
